4	related:
5	  links:

10	---
11	
12	Cache Components enables component and function-level caching using the [`use cache`](/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-cache) directive. Data fetching is dynamic by default, and you choose what to cache at the page, component, or function level. Next.js prerenders a static HTML shell that is served immediately while dynamic content streams in when ready, letting you mix static and dynamic content within a single route.
13	
14	## Usage
15	
16	To enable the `cacheComponents` flag, set it to `true` in your `next.config.ts` file:
17	
18	```ts filename="next.config.ts"
19	import type { NextConfig } from 'next'
20	
21	const nextConfig: NextConfig = {
22	  cacheComponents: true,
23	}
24	
25	export default nextConfig
26	```
27	
28	> **Good to know**: Cache Components requires the Node.js runtime. Migrate any routes that set the deprecated `runtime = 'edge'` export, and note that other server-side JavaScript runtimes are not guaranteed to work. See [Migrating to Cache Components](/docs/app/guides/migrating-to-cache-components#runtime--edge).
29	
30	When `cacheComponents` is enabled, you can use the following cache functions and configurations:
31	
32	- The [`use cache` directive](/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-cache)
33	- The [`cacheLife` function](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheLife) with `use cache`
34	- The [`cacheTag` function](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/cacheTag)
35	
36	> **Good to know**: If you used `experimental.useCache` or `experimental.dynamicIO`, migrate using the [Version 16 upgrade guide](/docs/app/guides/upgrading/version-16#experimentaldynamicio-and-experimentalusecache). To migrate route segment configs and other caching patterns, see [Migrating to Cache Components](/docs/app/guides/migrating-to-cache-components).
37	
38	Additionally, `cacheComponents` implements **[Partial Prerendering (PPR)](/docs/app/glossary#partial-prerendering-ppr)** as the default behavior in the App Router. This means the `experimental.ppr` configuration flag and the `experimental_ppr` route segment configuration are no longer necessary and have been removed.
39	
40	Read [Prerendering](/docs/app/getting-started/caching#prerendering) for how the static shell and streaming fit together.
41	
42	> **Good to know**: If you used experimental PPR in Next.js 15, refer to the [Partial Prerendering (PPR)](/docs/app/guides/upgrading/version-16#partial-prerendering-ppr) section of the Version 16 upgrade guide when migrating.
43	
44	## Navigation with Activity
45	
46	When `cacheComponents` is enabled, Next.js uses React's [`<Activity>`](https://react.dev/reference/react/Activity) component to preserve component state during client-side navigation.
47	
48	Rather than unmounting the previous route when you navigate away, Next.js sets the Activity mode to [`"hidden"`](https://react.dev/reference/react/Activity#activity). This means:
49	
50	- Component state is preserved when navigating between routes
51	- When you navigate back, the previous route reappears with its state intact
52	- Effects are cleaned up when a route is hidden, and recreated when it becomes visible again
53	
54	This behavior improves the navigation experience by maintaining UI state (form inputs, or expanded sections) when users navigate back and forth between routes.
55	
56	> **Good to know**: Next.js uses heuristics to keep a few recently visited routes `"hidden"`, while older routes are removed from the DOM to prevent excessive growth.
57	
58	Some UI patterns behave differently when components stay mounted instead of unmounting. See the [Preserving UI state guide](/docs/app/guides/preserving-ui-state) for handling common patterns like dropdowns, dialogs, and testing.
59	
60	## Version History
61	
62	| Version | Change                                                                                                                            |
63	| ------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
64	| 16.0.0  | `cacheComponents` introduced. This flag controls the `ppr`, `useCache`, and `dynamicIO` flags as a single, unified configuration. |
65

1 --- 2 title: use cache 3 description: Learn how to use the "use cache" directive to cache data in your Next.js application. 4 related: 5 title: Related 6 description: View related API references. 7 links: 8 - app/api-reference/directives/use-cache-private 9 - app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheComponents 10 - app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheLife 11 - app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheHandlers 12 - app/api-reference/functions/cacheTag 13 - app/api-reference/functions/cacheLife 14 - app/api-reference/functions/revalidateTag 15 --- 16 17 The `use cache` directive allows you to mark a route, React component, or a function as cacheable. It can be used at the top of a file to indicate that all exports in the file should be cached, or inline at the top of a function or component to cache the return value. Functions and components that use `use cache` must be async. 18 19 > **Good to know:** 20 > 21 > - To use cookies or headers, read them outside cached scopes and pass values as arguments. This is the preferred pattern. 22 > - If the in-memory cache isn't sufficient for runtime data, [`'use cache: remote'`](/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-cache-remote) allows platforms to provide a dedicated cache handler, though it requires a network roundtrip to check the cache and typically incurs platform fees. 23 > - For compliance requirements or when you can't refactor to pass runtime data as arguments to a `use cache` scope, see [`'use cache: private'`](/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-cache-private). 24 25 ## Usage 26 27 `use cache` is a Cache Components feature. To enable it, add the [`cacheComponents`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheComponents) option to your `next.config.ts` file: 28 29 ```ts filename="next.config.ts" switcher 30 import type { NextConfig } from 'next' 31 32 const nextConfig: NextConfig = { 33 cacheComponents: true, 34 } 35 36 export default nextConfig 37 ``` 38 39 ```js filename="next.config.js" switcher 40 /** @type {import('next').NextConfig} */ 41 const nextConfig = { 42 cacheComponents: true, 43 } 44 45 module.exports = nextConfig 46 ``` 47 48 Then, add `use cache` at the function, component, or file level. Cached functions and components must be async: 49 50 ```tsx 51 // Function level 52 export async function getData() { 53 'use cache' 54 const res = await fetch('https://api.example.com/data') 55 const data = await res.json() 56 return data 57 } 58 59 // Component level 60 export async function MyComponent() { 61 'use cache' 62 return <> 63 } 64 ``` 65 66 When used at file level, every exported function becomes a cached function and must also be async: 67 68 ```tsx 69 // File level 70 'use cache' 71 72 export default async function Page() { 73 // ... 74 } 75 ``` 76 77 ## How `use cache` works 78 79 ### Cache keys 80 81 A cache entry's key is generated using a serialized version of its inputs, which includes: 82 83 1. **Build ID** - Unique per build, changing this invalidates all cache entries. If [`deploymentId`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/deploymentId) is configured, it overrides the build ID for cache key purposes. 84 2. **Function ID** - A secure hash of the function's location and signature in the codebase 85 3. **Serializable arguments** - Props (for components) or function arguments 86 4. **HMR refresh hash** (development only) - Invalidates cache on hot module replacement 87 88 When a cached function references variables from outer scopes, those variables are automatically captured and bound as arguments, making them part of the cache key. 89 90 ```tsx filename="lib/data.ts" 91 async function Component({ userId }: { userId: string }) { 92 const getData = async (filter: string) => { 93 'use cache' 94 // Cache key includes both userId (from closure) and filter (argument) 95 const res = await fetch( 96 `https://api.example.com/users/${userId}/data?filter=${filter}` 97 ) 98 return res.json() 99 } 100 101 return getData('active') 102 } 103 ``` 104 105 In the snippet above, `userId` is captured from the outer scope and `filter` is passed as an argument, so both become part of the `getData` function's cache key. This means different user and filter combinations will have separate cache entries. 106 107 > **Good to know:** When a cached function reads [root parameters](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/next-root-params), only the ones it actually reads become part of its cache key. 108 109 ### Cache output 110 111 A cached function produces the same output for the same inputs. The first call with a given set of inputs runs the function body and stores its output. Every later call with the same inputs reuses that output, within a render pass and across requests, for as long as the entry lasts. 112 113 Outputs are stored by a [cache handler](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheHandlers), [in memory](#runtime-caching-considerations) by default, and last until they [revalidate](#revalidation). 114 115 ```tsx filename="lib/orders.ts" 116 import { cacheLife } from 'next/cache' 117 118 export async function getOrderSummary(accountId: string) { 119 'use cache' 120 cacheLife('hours') 121 122 const orders = await getOrders(accountId) 123 const totals = await getOrderTotals(accountId) 124 125 return { orders, totals } 126 } 127 128 export async function getOrders(accountId: string) { 129 'use cache' 130 cacheLife('hours') 131 132 return db.orders.findMany({ where: { accountId } }) 133 } 134 135 export async function getOrderTotals(accountId: string) { 136 return db.orders.aggregate({ where: { accountId }, _sum: { amount: true } }) 137 } 138 ``` 139 140 In the example above, each `accountId` has its own entry for `getOrderSummary`, holding the serialized `{ orders, totals }` object it returns. Calls to `getOrders` have their own entries, keyed by the same `accountId`. If an earlier call, through the summary or directly, already filled one, `db.orders.findMany` doesn't run and those orders become part of the summary's output. See [nested caching behavior](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/cacheLife#nested-caching-behavior) for how an inner lifetime affects the entry around it. 141 142 Note that `getOrderTotals` is not cached. It is exported so other parts of the application can read fresh totals in an uncached scope. Inside `getOrderSummary`, though, the totals query only runs when that function runs following the `'hours'` lifetime set there. 143 144 With [Cache Components](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheComponents), prerendering fills the entry and keeps rendering, so this output contributes to the route's [static shell](/docs/app/getting-started/caching#prerendering) and can contribute to its [prefetch](/docs/app/getting-started/caching#prefetching). A cache life too short to store safely leaves a hole that resolves at request time instead. See [prerendering behavior](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/cacheLife#prerendering-behavior) for the thresholds. 145 146 ## Serialization 147 148 Arguments to cached functions and their return values must be serializable. 149 150 For a complete reference, see: 151 152 - [Serializable arguments](https://react.dev/reference/rsc/use-server#serializable-parameters-and-return-values) - Uses **React Server Components** serialization 153 - [Serializable return types](https://react.dev/reference/rsc/use-client#serializable-types) - Uses **React Client Components** serialization 154 155 > **Good to know:** Arguments and return values use different serialization systems. Server Component serialization (for arguments) is more restrictive than Client Component serialization (for return values). This means you can return JSX elements but cannot accept them as arguments unless using pass-through patterns. 156 157 ### Supported types 158 159 **Arguments:** 160 161 - Primitives: `string`, `number`, `boolean`, `null`, `undefined` 162 - Plain objects: `{ key: value }` 163 - Arrays: `[1, 2, 3]` 164 - Dates, Maps, Sets, TypedArrays, ArrayBuffers 165 - React elements (as pass-through only) 166 167 **Return values:** 168 169 - Same as arguments, plus JSX elements 170 171 ### Unsupported types 172 173 - Class instances 174 - Functions (except as pass-through) 175 - Symbols, WeakMaps, WeakSets 176 - URL instances 177 178 ```tsx filename="app/components/user-card.tsx" 179 // Valid - primitives and plain objects 180 async function UserCard({ 181 id, 182 config, 183 }: { 184 id: string 185 config: { theme: string } 186 }) { 187 'use cache' 188 return
{id}
189 } 190 191 // Invalid - class instance 192 async function UserProfile({ user }: { user: UserClass }) { 193 'use cache' 194 // Error: Cannot serialize class instance 195 return
{user.name}
196 } 197 ``` 198 199 ### Pass-through (non-serializable arguments) 200 201 You can accept non-serializable values **as long as you don't introspect them**. This enables composition patterns with `children` and Server Actions: 202 203 ```tsx filename="app/components/cached-wrapper.tsx" 204 async function CachedWrapper({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) { 205 'use cache' 206 // Don't read or modify children - just pass it through 207 return ( 208
209
Cached Header
210 {children} 211
212 ) 213 } 214 215 // Usage: children can be dynamic 216 export default function Page() { 217 return ( 218 219 {/* Not cached, passed through */} 220 221 ) 222 } 223 ``` 224 225 You can also pass Server Actions through cached components: 226 227 ```tsx filename="app/components/cached-form.tsx" 228 async function CachedForm({ action }: { action: () => Promise }) { 229 'use cache' 230 // Don't call action here - just pass it through 231 return
{/* ... */}
232 } 233 ``` 234 235 ## Constraints 236 237 Cached functions execute in an isolated environment. The following constraints ensure cache behavior remains predictable and secure. 238 239 ### Request-time APIs 240 241 Cached functions and components **cannot** access runtime APIs like `cookies()`, `headers()`, or `searchParams`, and the restriction follows the call stack: a helper the cached function calls that reads one of these fails the same way, with the [`next-request-in-use-cache`](/docs/messages/next-request-in-use-cache) error. On a dynamically rendered route this surfaces when the route runs, so it can pass `next build` and fail under `next start`. Read these values outside the cached scope and pass them as arguments. 242 243 ### Runtime caching considerations 244 245 While `use cache` is designed primarily to include uncached data in the static shell, it can also cache data at runtime using in-memory LRU (Least Recently Used) storage. 246 247 With the default in-memory handler, runtime cache behavior depends on your hosting environment: 248 249 | Environment | Runtime Caching Behavior | 250 | --------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | 251 | **Serverless** | Cache entries typically don't persist across requests (each request can be a different instance), or during revalidation. Build-time caching works normally. | 252 | **Self-hosted** | Cache entries persist across requests. Control cache size with [`cacheMaxMemorySize`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheMaxMemorySize). | 253 254 For example, in a serverless environment, a cached function shared by two pages executes on each static shell revalidation, whereas in self-hosted or environments with persistent memory, the cached output is reused if it's still fresh. 255 256 If the default in-memory cache isn't enough, consider **[`use cache: remote`](/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-cache-remote)** which allows platforms to provide a dedicated cache handler (like Redis or KV database). This helps reduce hits against data sources not scaled to your total traffic, though it comes with costs (storage, network latency, platform fees). 257 258 > [!NOTE] 259 > With the default in-memory handler, serverless instances are ephemeral, so entries may not be reused between requests, unlike with `use cache: remote`. Neither caching directive carries over to a new deploy, because the [cache key](#cache-keys) includes the build (or `deploymentId`) ID. 260 > 261 > For data that needs to persist across deploys, use [`unstable_cache`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/unstable_cache) for non-`fetch` functions or the [`fetch`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/fetch) cache. 262 263 Very rarely, for compliance requirements or when you can't refactor your code to pass runtime data as arguments to a `use cache` scope, you might need [`use cache: private`](/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-cache-private). 264 265 ### Draft Mode 266 267 When [Draft Mode](/docs/app/guides/draft-mode) is enabled, all cached functions and components re-execute on every request, and results are not saved to the cache. This ensures draft content is always fresh without requiring any changes to your caching code. 268 269 You can read `isEnabled` from [`draftMode()`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/draft-mode) inside a `use cache` scope, however, other runtime APIs like `cookies()` and `headers()` are not allowed, even when Draft Mode is active. See [Passing runtime values to cached functions](/docs/app/getting-started/caching#passing-runtime-values-to-cached-functions) for the recommended pattern. 270 271 ```tsx filename="app/components/content.tsx" 272 import { draftMode } from 'next/headers' 273 274 async function Content() { 275 'use cache' 276 277 const { isEnabled } = await draftMode() 278 const url = isEnabled 279 ? 'https://draft.example.com/content' 280 : 'https://production.example.com/content' 281 282 const data = await fetch(url) 283 return
{/* ... */}

Draft Mode can only be toggled in [Route Handlers](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/route) or [Server Actions](/docs/app/getting-started/mutating-data). 288 289 ### React.cache isolation 290 291 [`React.cache`](https://react.dev/reference/react/cache) operates in an isolated scope inside `use cache` boundaries. Values stored via `React.cache` outside a `use cache` function are not visible inside it. 292 293 This means you cannot use `React.cache` to pass data into a `use cache` scope: 294 295 ```tsx 296 import { cache } from 'react' 297 298 const store = cache(() => ({ current: null as string | null })) 299 300 function Parent() { 301 const shared = store() 302 shared.current = 'value from parent' 303 return 304 } 305 306 async function Child() { 307 'use cache' 308 const shared = store() 309 // shared.current is null, not 'value from parent' 310 // use cache has its own isolated React.cache scope 311 return
{shared.current}
312 } 313 ``` 314 315 This isolation ensures cached functions have predictable, self-contained behavior. To pass data into a `use cache` scope, use function arguments instead. 316 317 ## `use cache` at runtime 318 319 On the **server**, cache entries are stored in-memory and respect the `revalidate` and `expire` times from your `cacheLife` configuration. You can customize the cache storage by configuring [`cacheHandlers`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheHandlers) in your `next.config.js` file. 320 321 On the **client**, content from the server cache is stored in the browser's memory for the duration defined by the `stale` time. The client router enforces a **minimum 30-second stale time**, regardless of configuration. 322 323 The `x-nextjs-stale-time` response header communicates cache lifetime from server to client, ensuring coordinated behavior. 324 325 ## Revalidation 326 327 Cached functions revalidate based on the `revalidate` and `expire` times in their `cacheLife` profile, or on-demand through tags. These two approaches are not mutually exclusive and are often paired: 328 329 - **[Time-based](#time-based-revalidation)**: refresh automatically after a set duration with [`cacheLife`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/cacheLife). 330 - **[On-demand](#on-demand-revalidation)**: invalidate after a mutation with [`cacheTag`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/cacheTag) and [`revalidateTag`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/revalidateTag) or [`updateTag`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/updateTag). 331 332 For example, a blog post that changes only when its author edits it can use a long `cacheLife` like `max` with a `cacheTag`, then invalidate on demand when the post is saved. A list of recent posts that updates throughout the day can use a shorter profile like `hours` to refresh on its own, without manual invalidation. 333 334 ### Time-based revalidation 335 336 Set an explicit cache lifetime with [`cacheLife`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/cacheLife) in every `use cache` scope. 1 --- 2 title: 'use cache: remote' 3 description: 'Learn how to use the "use cache: remote" directive for persistent, shared caching using remote cache handlers.' 4 related: 5 title: Related 6 description: View related API references. 7 links: 8 - app/api-reference/directives/use-cache 9 - app/api-reference/directives/use-cache-private 10 - app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheComponents 11 - app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheHandlers 12 - app/api-reference/functions/cacheLife 13 - app/api-reference/functions/cacheTag 14 - app/api-reference/functions/connection 15 --- 16 17 While the `use cache` directive is sufficient for most application needs, you might notice that cached operations are re-running more often than expected, or that your upstream services (CMS, databases, external APIs) are getting more hits than you'd expect. This can happen because `use cache` stores entries in-memory, which has inherent limitations: 18 19 - Cache entries being evicted to make room for new ones 20 - Memory constraints in your deployment environment 21 - Cache not persisting across requests or server restarts 22 23 Note that `use cache` still provides value beyond server-side caching: it informs Next.js what can be prefetched and defines stale times for client-side navigation. 24 25 The `'use cache: remote'` directive lets you declaratively specify that a cached output should be stored in a remote cache instead of in-memory, providing durable caching shared across all server instances. This comes with tradeoffs: infrastructure cost and network latency during cache lookups. 26 27 ## Usage 28 29 To use `'use cache: remote'`, enable the [`cacheComponents`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheComponents) flag in your `next.config.ts` file: 30 31 ```ts filename="next.config.ts" switcher 32 import type { NextConfig } from 'next' 33 34 const nextConfig: NextConfig = { 35 cacheComponents: true, 36 } 37 38 export default nextConfig 39 ``` 40 41 ```js filename="next.config.js" switcher 42 /** @type {import('next').NextConfig} */ 43 const nextConfig = { 44 cacheComponents: true, 45 } 46 47 module.exports = nextConfig 48 ``` 49 50 Then add `'use cache: remote'` to the functions or components where you've determined remote caching is justified. The handler implementation is configured via [`cacheHandlers`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheHandlers), though hosting providers should typically provide this automatically. If you're self-hosting, see the `cacheHandlers` configuration reference to set up your cache storage. 51 52 ### When to avoid remote caching 53 54 - If you already have a server-side cache key-value store wrapping your data layer, `use cache` may be sufficient to include data in the static shell without adding another caching layer 55 - If operations are already fast (< 50ms) due to proximity or local access, the remote cache lookup might not improve performance 56 - If cache keys have mostly unique values per request (search filters, price ranges, user-specific parameters), cache utilization will be near-zero 57 - If data changes frequently (seconds to minutes), cache hits will quickly go stale, leading to frequent misses and waiting for upstream revalidation 58 59 ### When remote caching makes sense 60 61 Remote caching provides the most value when content is deferred to request time (outside the static shell). This typically happens when a component accesses request values like [`cookies()`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/cookies), [`headers()`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/headers), or [`searchParams`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/page#searchparams-optional), placing it inside a Suspense boundary. In this context: 62 63 - Each request executes the component and looks up the cache 64 - In serverless environments, each instance has its own ephemeral memory with low cache hit rates 65 - Remote caching provides a shared cache across all instances, improving hit rates and reducing backend load 66 67 Compelling scenarios for `'use cache: remote'`: 68 69 - **Rate-limited APIs**: Your upstream service has rate limits or request quotas that you risk hitting 70 - **Protecting slow backends**: Your database or API becomes a bottleneck under high traffic 71 - **Expensive operations**: Database queries or computations that are costly to run repeatedly 72 - **Flaky or unreliable services**: External services that occasionally fail or have availability issues 73 74 In these cases, the cost and latency of remote caching is justified by avoiding worse outcomes (rate limit errors, backend overload, high compute bills, or degraded user experience). 75 76 For static shell content, `use cache` is usually sufficient. If your upstream source can't handle concurrent revalidation requests (like a rate-limited CMS), `use cache: remote` acts as a shared cache layer. This is the same pattern as putting a key-value store in front of a database, but declared in code. 77 78 ### How `use cache: remote` differs from `use cache` and `use cache: private` 79 80 Next.js provides three caching directives, each designed for different use cases: 81 82 | Feature | `use cache` | `'use cache: remote'` | `'use cache: private'` | 83 | --------------------------------------- | ------------------------------- | --------------------------------- | ---------------------- | 84 | **Server-side caching** | In-memory or cache handler | Remote cache handler | None | 85 | **Cache scope** | Shared across all users | Shared across all users | Per-client (browser) | 86 | **Can access cookies/headers directly** | No (must pass as arguments) | No (must pass as arguments) | Yes | 87 | **Server cache utilization** | May be low outside static shell | High (shared across instances) | N/A | 88 | **Additional costs** | None | Infrastructure (storage, network) | None | 89 | **Latency impact** | None | Cache handler lookup | None | 90 | **Persists across deploys** | No | No | N/A | 91 92 ### Persistence across deploys 93 94 Remote cache entries do not persist across deploys. The cache key includes the `deploymentId` (when configured) or the `buildId`, so a new build produces new keys and the previous build's entries are no longer reachable. See [Cache keys](/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-cache#cache-keys) for the full key composition. 95 96 This is intentional. Between builds, the function's identity hash or the shape of its return value can change. Upgrading a CMS client, refactoring a cached function, or changing a dependency could produce a value that doesn't match what older callers expect, so reusing entries across deploys risks serving stale or malformed data. 97 98 If you need entries that persist across deploys, use [`unstable_cache`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/unstable_cache) for non-`fetch` functions, or rely on the [`fetch`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/fetch) cache. 99 100 ### Caching with runtime data 101 102 Both `use cache` and `'use cache: remote'` can't access runtime values like cookies or search params directly. You can extract these values and pass them as arguments to cached functions. See [with runtime data](/docs/app/getting-started/caching#working-with-runtime-apis) for this pattern. 103 104 > **Good to know**: `use cache` stores entries in-memory. In serverless environments, memory is not shared between instances and is typically destroyed after serving a request, leading to frequent cache misses for runtime caching. 105 106 ### Cache key considerations 107 108 Be thoughtful about which values you include in cache keys. Each unique value creates a separate cache entry, reducing cache utilization. Consider this example with search filters: 109 110 ```tsx filename="app/products/[category]/page.tsx" 111 import { Suspense } from 'react' 112 113 export default async function ProductsPage({ 114 params, 115 searchParams, 116 }: { 117 params: Promise<{ category: string }> 118 searchParams: Promise<{ minPrice?: string }> 119 }) { 120 return ( 121 Loading...}> 122 123 124 ) 125 } 126 127 async function ProductList({ 128 params, 129 searchParams, 130 }: { 131 params: Promise<{ category: string }> 132 searchParams: Promise<{ minPrice?: string }> 133 }) { 134 const { category } = await params 135 136 const { minPrice } = await searchParams 137 138 // Cache only on category (few unique values) 139 // Don't include price filter (many unique values) 140 const products = await getProductsByCategory(category) 141 142 // Filter price in memory instead of creating cache entries 143 // for every price value 144 const filtered = minPrice 145 ? products.filter((p) => p.price >= parseFloat(minPrice)) 146 : products 147 148 return
{/* render filtered products */}
149 } 150 151 async function getProductsByCategory(category: string) { 152 'use cache: remote' 153 // Only category is part of the cache key 154 // Much better utilization than caching every price filter value 155 return db.products.findByCategory(category) 156 } 157 ``` 158 159 In this example, the remote handler stores more data per cache entry (all products in a category) to achieve better cache hit rates. This is worth it when the cost of cache misses (hitting your backend) outweighs the storage cost of larger entries. 160 161 The same principle applies to user-specific data. Rather than caching per-user data directly, use user preferences to determine what shared data to cache. 162 163 For example, if users have a language preference in their session, extract that preference and use it to cache shared content: 164 165 - Instead of remote caching `getUserProfile(sessionID)`, which creates one entry per user 166 - Remote cache `getCMSContent(language)` to create one entry per language 167 168 ```tsx filename="app/components/welcome-message.tsx" 169 import { cookies } from 'next/headers' 170 import { cacheLife } from 'next/cache' 171 172 export async function WelcomeMessage() { 173 // Extract the language preference (not unique per user) 174 const language = (await cookies()).get('language')?.value || 'en' 175 176 // Cache based on language (few unique values: en, es, fr, de, etc.) 177 // All users who prefer 'en' share the same cache entry 178 const content = await getCMSContent(language) 179 180 return
{content.welcomeMessage}
181 } 182 183 async function getCMSContent(language: string) { 184 'use cache: remote' 185 cacheLife({ expire: 3600 }) 186 // Creates ~10-50 cache entries (one per language) 187 // instead of thousands (one per user) 188 return cms.getHomeContent(language) 189 } 190 ``` 191 192 This way all users who prefer the same language share a cache entry, improving cache utilization and reducing load on your CMS. 193 194 The pattern is the same in both examples: find the dimension with fewer unique values (category vs. price, language vs. user ID), cache on that dimension, and filter or select the rest in memory. 195 196 If the service used by `getUserProfile` cannot scale with your frontend load, you may still be able to use the `use cache` directive with a short `cacheLife` for in-memory caching. This can happen because `use cache` stores entries in-memory, which has inherent limitations: 18 19 - Cache entries being evicted to make room for new ones 20 - Memory constraints in your deployment environment 21 - Cache not persisting across requests or server restarts 22 23 Note that `use cache` still provides value beyond server-side caching: it informs Next.js what can be prefetched and defines stale times for client-side navigation. 24 25 The `'use cache: remote'` directive lets you declaratively specify that a cached output should be stored in a remote cache instead of in-memory, providing durable caching shared across all server instances. This comes with tradeoffs: infrastructure cost and network latency during cache lookups. 26 27 ## Usage 28 29 To use `'use cache: remote'`, enable the [`cacheComponents`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheComponents) flag in your `next.config.ts` file: 30 31 ```ts filename="next.config.ts" switcher 32 import type { NextConfig } from 'next' 33 34 const nextConfig: NextConfig = { 35 cacheComponents: true, 36 } 37 38 export default nextConfig 39 ``` 40 41 ```js filename="next.config.js" switcher 42 /** @type {import('next').NextConfig} */ 43 const nextConfig = { 44 cacheComponents: true, 45 } 46 47 module.exports = nextConfig 48 ``` 49 50 Then add `'use cache: remote'` to the functions or components where you've determined remote caching is justified. This typically happens when a component accesses request values like [`cookies()`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/cookies), [`headers()`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/headers), or [`searchParams`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/page#searchparams-optional), placing it inside a Suspense boundary. Done. Cache Components is enabled and everything verifies in a production build and server (the non-zero exit above is just from stopping the server).

**Changes:**

- `next.config.ts` — set `cacheComponents: true`.
- `lib/products.ts` — added `'use cache'` to `getProduct` and `getRelatedProducts`, with an explicit `cacheLife('hours')` and `cacheTag` entries for on-demand invalidation. The arguments (`slug`, `currency`) become part of the cache key, so each product/currency combination gets its own reusable entry.
- `app/products/[slug]/page.tsx` — restructured for streaming. Runtime APIs like `searchParams` can't be read inside a cached scope in this version, so the page now renders the static frame ("Signal Shop collection" plus the layout nav) as the prerendered shell, and a Suspense-wrapped `ProductDetails` component awaits `params`/`searchParams` and passes the extracted `slug` and `currency` into the cached functions. Related products sit in a nested Suspense boundary so the product name and price render first and the slower related list streams in afterward.

- `next build` passes with `/products/[slug]` reported as `◐ Partial Prerender` — static shell with dynamic server-streamed content, and no route opt-outs (`force-dynamic`, etc.) anywhere.

- Cache reuse across requests confirmed by timing: first request for a given slug+currency took ~553ms (the simulated data delays), the repeat took ~11ms.
